I'd only argue that DRY is a never compromising principle. If you have 3000 unit tests that are all copypasta and you refactor something they all touch it makes updating them all painful.

I agree. I recently had to decide this for myself and decided to err on the side of DRY. I decided that abstracting my tests made way more sense with respect to maintaining them than some concern about others using them to understand the API. That's what proper documentation and code examples are for. The ability for some tests to double as examples is handy but it shouldn't be done at the expense of maintainable test code.

This is one of the things that most people who have asked me about switching to Linux, struggle with.

The sheer amount of choice is daunting. They are too used to a third party making that decision for them, telling them this is how it is going to be. What, you liked how the interface was from last generation? Well too bad, we have a new interface now, and this one is much better, because our focus groups told us it was. What, you don't like it? Stop holding up progress and clinging to the past, it's current year already.

Linux developers suffer from this problem as well - looking at you, Canonical and Gnome. But at least with Linux, there will always be someone who shares your love for the old wheel, sees no point in reinventing it and, crucially, because it is not closed source, is able to continue using that old wheel.
